sections.markdown:
**Think of Dio as the FedEx pickup truck for your app's data.**

The stock `http` package is like walking to the post office yourself — one package at a time, hand-write the address, no receipt, no retries if the address is wrong.

Dio is FedEx:
- **BaseOptions** — the pre-printed return address on every package (baseUrl, timeouts, default headers).
- **Interceptors** — the sorting-facility conveyor belt. Every package passes through: stamp with tracking, sniff for hazardous contents (auth token), retry-3-times bin if delivery fails, incident-log carbon copy.
- **CancelToken** — the panic button on your phone that recalls a truck mid-route. When the user leaves the screen, you press it; every package still in transit gets returned before it hits the destination.
- **FormData / MultipartFile** — the special-handling packaging for photos + docs.
- **Custom Adapter** — swap the FedEx truck for a Ferrari (native HTTP), a mock (unit tests), or a MITM proxy (Charles for debugging).

**Why every Flutter app > MVP switches to Dio:** production HTTP needs cross-cutting concerns (auth, retry, logging, analytics, mock) applied to *every* call. Sprinkling those into 40 call sites is a maintenance disaster. Dio's interceptor chain lets you write them ONCE and every request/response passes through. Also — cancellation. On mobile, users leave screens constantly; without cancel-on-dispose you leak sockets + setState-after-dispose crashes.

**Dio** is the de-facto Flutter HTTP client — powerful `BaseOptions`, chainable `Interceptor`s, `FormData`, `MultipartFile` uploads with progress, `CancelToken`, request/response transformers, custom `HttpClientAdapter` (Cronet on Android, native URLSession on iOS), and a testable `MockAdapter`. Written in pure Dart with pluggable IO. **Pub.dev** points ~85 % of new Flutter projects choose Dio when interceptor chains, timeouts, or upload-progress matter.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: One global Dio, no CancelTokens.** User leaves screen, requests keep running, `setState` after `dispose` crashes. Always attach a per-screen CancelToken + cancel in `dispose`.
**Mistake 2: Wrong interceptor order.** Retry BEFORE Auth = retries send stale token; Log INSIDE Auth = you don't see the final `Authorization` header. Rule: Log outermost → Auth → Retry innermost.

**Mistake 3: Token refresh storm.** 10 parallel requests all hit 401, each calls `refresh` → 10 refresh calls, backend rate-limits, chaos. Serialize refresh via a shared `Future` — first caller starts it, rest await the same future.

**Mistake 4: `validateStatus` default.** By default Dio throws on any non-2xx. If you handle 4xx as data (form validation), set `validateStatus: (s) => s < 500` — otherwise you catch what should be normal response flow.
**Mistake 5: Logging sensitive data.** `PrettyDioLogger(requestBody: true)` in production dumps passwords + tokens to logcat. Gate with `kDebugMode`.
**Mistake 6: Retrying non-idempotent POSTs.** Blindly retrying `POST /orders` = duplicate orders. Retry only GET / PUT / DELETE, or require an `Idempotency-Key` header on POST.
**Mistake 7: No timeouts.** Default `connectTimeout` is null (infinite). App hangs forever on flaky 3G. Always set connect/send/receive.
**Mistake 8: Reusing `RequestOptions` after `fetch`.** Mutating `extra` on the same options across retries corrupts state. Clone before mutating.
## Best practices
**1. One Dio per API host** — different baseUrls, different auth, different interceptor stacks. Not one globalDio for everything.
**2. Interceptors for cross-cutting concerns** — auth, retry, log, cache, analytics. Not in call sites.
**3. CancelToken per screen / per query key** — cancel on dispose or on parameter change.
**4. Typed AppError via `mapDioError`** — call sites handle `NetworkError` / `AuthError` / `ValidationError`, not raw `DioException`.
**5. Serialize token refresh** via a shared Future/Completer.
**6. Set all three timeouts** — connect, send, receive.
**7. Use `Native Adapter` (Cronet / URLSession)** for HTTP/2 + QUIC + system trust store.
**8. Test with `http_mock_adapter`** — no real network in unit tests.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy)** — Configure Dio + baseUrl + timeouts + logger; hit a JSON endpoint.
**Practice 2 (Medium)** — AuthInterceptor with Bearer + 401-refresh; verify retry with `http_mock_adapter`.
**Practice 3 (Medium)** — Serialize concurrent 401s → single refresh.
**Practice 4 (Hard)** — Screen-scoped CancelToken; cancel on route pop mid-request.
**Practice 5 (Hard)** — Multipart upload with progress bar + retry on network failure only.
**Practice 6 (Expert)** — Swap adapter to `native_dio_adapter` (Cronet + URLSession); benchmark cold-start.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: Why Dio over the built-in http package?**

**A:** `http` is minimal — one request at a time, no cross-cutting hooks. Dio adds **interceptor chain** (auth, retry, log, cache — all applied once, not per call site), **BaseOptions** (single source for baseUrl + timeouts + headers), **CancelToken** (cancel on screen dispose — critical to avoid setState-after-dispose), **FormData / MultipartFile** (uploads with progress), **response transformers** (auto JSON decode + custom types), **custom adapters** (mock in tests, native HTTP/2/QUIC in prod). Any real app hits at least 3 of those needs within the first month, so most teams pick Dio on day one. The **cost** is a bigger API surface + one more dependency; `http` remains a fine choice for tiny apps or platform-agnostic libraries.

**Q2: Walk through interceptor ordering — what goes where and why?**

**A:** Interceptors run in **add-order on the request side**, **reverse-order on the response side**. So `[Log, Auth, Retry]` means: request goes Log → Auth → Retry → network; response comes back Retry → Auth → Log. Correct order: **Log outermost** so it sees the final headers (with token) and the final response (after retries). **Auth in the middle** — attaches token to request, refreshes on 401 response. **Retry innermost** — closest to the network; retries only network/5xx errors before Auth even sees them. If you flip Auth and Retry, Retry retries with a stale token (bad). If Log is innermost, it misses the token stamp (misleading debugging). Some teams add a **Cache** interceptor before Retry — cached hits skip both retry + network.

**Q3: How do you cancel in-flight requests correctly?**

**A:** Pass a `CancelToken` on every request; **cancel in `dispose`**. On cancellation, Dio throws `DioException` with `type: DioExceptionType.cancel` — catch and swallow (it's expected). **Two patterns:** **(1) Per-screen** — one CancelToken per State, cancel in `dispose`. Works when a screen has a handful of requests. **(2) Per-query-key** — a Map of CancelTokens keyed by (screen, query params); when params change (e.g. search text), cancel the old token, spawn a new one, prevents result races. **Also:** always check `mounted` before `setState` on the resolved future — cancellation raced with completion is possible. **In tests:** await + `expectLater(future, throwsA(isA<DioException>()))`. Getting cancellation right eliminates the most common Flutter crash class.

**Q4: How do you handle 401 with token refresh — including the race?**

**A:** **(1) Refresh interceptor** intercepts 401 responses. **(2) Refresh serially** — use a shared `Completer<void>` or `Future<void>`. First 401 sets it + calls `/refresh`; subsequent 401s await the same future rather than each triggering their own refresh. **(3) Retry the original request** with the new token — clone `RequestOptions`, mark `extra['retried'] = true` (prevents infinite loop if refresh returns a still-bad token), fetch it. **(4) Refresh failure** — surface the original 401, force logout, clear tokens. **(5) Idempotent guard** — only retry GET/PUT/DELETE; POST needs an `Idempotency-Key`. **(6) Skip refresh interceptor for the /refresh endpoint itself** — otherwise infinite recursion. Every senior interviewer digs into 'what if 10 requests all hit 401 at once' — 'we serialize on a shared future' is the target answer.

**Q5: How do you test Dio-based code?**

**A:** Use `http_mock_adapter`. Replace the real HTTP adapter with a `DioAdapter` that returns canned responses per URL + method. **Advantages** over `HttpOverrides` or manual mocks: (1) matches on URL + method + query — clean intent. (2) can return different responses to consecutive calls of the same URL (test refresh flows). (3) supports throwing DioException to test retry logic. **Test strategy** — inject the Dio instance (or the wrapping API-client) via DI/Provider; in tests, construct one with the mock adapter. **Don't test the underlying network** — that's slow, flaky, and someone else's job. **Do test:** interceptor behavior (does 401 → refresh → retry succeed?), error mapping (`DioException` → typed `AppError`), cancellation. Also snapshot golden request payloads for critical endpoints.

**Q6: When would you swap the default HTTP adapter for Native (Cronet / URLSession)?**

**A:** Dio ships an **`IOHttpClientAdapter`** by default (Dart's `HttpClient`). Swap to `native_dio_adapter` for platform native stacks: **Cronet** on Android (Chrome's networking — HTTP/2, QUIC, connection pooling, background prefetch), **URLSession** on iOS (system trust store, background transfers, iOS-native TLS). **Wins:** (1) protocol upgrades (HTTP/2 multiplexing, QUIC on 5G), (2) system-level trust store (respects MDM CAs, corporate proxies), (3) shared connection pool with WebView / native libs, (4) background download continuation. **Costs:** larger APK (Cronet embed), platform-specific bugs, harder debugging. **Rule of thumb:** most apps are fine with the default; swap only after measuring on cellular / high-latency and seeing >100 ms wins from connection reuse or protocol upgrade. **Alternative for HTTPS pinning + intercept-proof security:** custom adapter wrapping BadCertificateCallback + `securityContext`.

## Real-world usage

- **Every mid-large Flutter app** — startup, e-commerce, banking, delivery.
- **Kills manual `try/catch`-in-every-widget** anti-pattern.
- **Analytics** — an interceptor that logs latency + status to Firebase Perf.
- **Offline sync** — an interceptor queues writes when offline + replays.
- **HTTPS pinning + MITM protection** — via custom adapter.
- **NOT the right tool for** — WebSocket (use `web_socket_channel`), gRPC (use `grpc` package), Firebase (its own SDK).

## Advanced notes

- **`dio_smart_retry`** — pre-built retry interceptor with exp backoff + jittering + idempotency guard.
- **`dio_cache_interceptor`** — HTTP cache spec + local persistence + stale-while-revalidate.
- **Response transformers** — hook JSON-decoding to a custom `fromJson` factory.
- **`Options.extra`** — pass metadata (retried flag, tenant id) alongside the request through interceptors.
- **`fetch(RequestOptions)`** vs high-level `get/post` — used when replaying a cloned request in interceptors.
- **Concurrent uploads** — cap via `Semaphore` in your API client; unbounded parallelism thrashes cellular.
- **HTTP/2 push** — supported via native adapter only.
- **Certificate pinning** — `SecurityContext.setTrustedCertificatesBytes` + wrap in a custom adapter.
- **Streaming responses** — `responseType: ResponseType.stream` for large downloads with `Stream<List<int>>`.
- **`onSendProgress` / `onReceiveProgress`** for UX bars.
- **Global exception hook** — wrap Dio in an `ApiClient` class; every call routes through one `handle()` that maps + logs to Crashlytics.
- **Retrofit codegen** — `retrofit_generator` builds a typed API surface on top of Dio.
